newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols well bid, driven by mark/yen.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols well bid, driven by mark/yen.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were firmer in U.S. trading, with a slide in spot mark/yen keeping mark/yen and dollar/yen options well bid, dealers said.
"You can blame it all on mark/yen, although dollar/yen itself has been moving up and down pretty well," said Masao Okada, chief dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.

The dollar floundered in the upper-120 yen area in U.S. morning trade, just above a one-month low overnight of 120.36, due partly to the yen's strength against the mark. Mark/yen broke out from a four-month-old triangle on Wednesday.

One-month dollar/yen implied volatility gained about 0.7 point on the day to 11.5/11.7 percent. The dollar/yen curve went back into a slight inversion, with three-month at 11.2/11.4 percent and one-year at 11.05/11.25.
Due to the lower liquidity in dollar/mark options market, some traders were seen to have bid up dollar/yen volatilities as a make-do hedge as mark/yen volatilities jumped.

One-month mark/yen volatility rose more than a full point to 10.4/10.8 percent. There was talk that a big hedge fund bought two billion marks' worth of one-month mark puts with a strike price of around 71 in early Asian trading overnight.

Dollar/mark volatilities were also firmer, even though spot was relatively narrow ranged, drifting near Wednesday's closing level just below 1.69 marks. One-month dollar/mark was marginally higher at 9.9/10.1 percent.

"We're still not that far from the highs in dollar/mark," said a U.S. bank trader. But he added that the inversion in the dollar/mark curve had flattened in the first few months as the short-dateds were pressured by time decay. Three-month stood at 9.9/10.1 percent, while one-year was at 9.65/9.75.
Traders said the dollar's violent rally to above 122.50 yen on Wednesday and a sharp reversal overnight buoyed the front end in dollar/yen.

"You have had a bi-directional market with pretty wide daily ranges, so it's natural that there's demand for gamma," Okada said. Shorter-dated options have high gamma and are sensitive to spot rate swings.

He noted that risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, were skewed toward yen calls in the front end but flat in the six-month area and favoring yen puts in further-out maturities.
He said the skews showed that the market was not totally convinced the dollar's long-term uptrend was over.

"If risk reversals flip toward yen calls in the back months and back-end volatilities start catching up with the front end, it could mean that the market is accepting the idea of a downtrend in the dollar," Okada said.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal for dollar/yen stood at 0.4/0.7 percent in favor of yen calls. In dollar/mark, one-month 25-delta was pegged at 0.0/0.4 percent skewed for mark puts.
